chunks: All things cannot be comprehended except through two means: through the senses and the heart. The senses comprehend through three modes: comprehension by penetration, comprehension by contact, and comprehension without penetration or contact.

As for comprehension by penetration, these are sounds, smells, and tastes. As for comprehension by contact, these are the recognition of shapes such as the square and the triangle, and recognition of softness and roughness, heat and cold. As for comprehension without contact or penetration, this is vision — for it perceives things without contact or penetration in any space other than its own, nor in its own space.

The comprehension of vision has a medium and a cause: its medium is the air and its cause is light. When the medium is continuous between it and the object seen, and the cause is present, one perceives what one faces of colours and figures. But when vision is directed at something for which there is no medium, it returns and reflects what is behind it — like a person looking in a mirror, whose vision does not pass through the mirror. When there is no medium for it, it returns and reflects what is behind it. Similarly, one who looks into clear water returns and reflects what is behind it, since there is no medium for the penetration of sight.

As for the heart, its domain is over the atmosphere (al-hawa'); it comprehends all that is in the atmosphere and imagines it. When the heart is directed at what does not exist in the atmosphere, it returns and reflects what is in the atmosphere. Therefore, it is not fitting for an intelligent person to direct his heart toward what does not exist in the atmosphere regarding the matter of Divine Unity (tawhid) — Mighty and Majestic is God — for if he does so, he will only imagine what exists in the atmosphere, just as we have described regarding vision. Exalted is God above any resemblance to His creation.

key_terms.الإدراك: Comprehension, perception — the central epistemological concept of the argument
key_terms.البصر: Vision/sight — the mode of perception that operates without penetration or contact
key_terms.التوحيد: Divine Unity (Tawhid) — the doctrine of God's absolute oneness, which requires transcending material cognition
key_terms.الحواسّ: The senses — the faculty through which material things are perceived
key_terms.القلب: The heart/intellect — in Islamic philosophy, the locus of cognition and understanding
key_terms.المداخلة: Penetration — the mode of perception where a substance enters the sensing organ (sound, smell, taste)
key_terms.المماسّة: Contact/touching — the mode of perception through physical touch
key_terms.الهواء: The atmosphere/air — the medium of perception and the domain of the heart

ai.seo_question: How did Hisham ibn al-Hakam explain the limits of human perception in understanding the Divine Unity?
ai.summary: Hisham ibn al-Hakam, the celebrated Shia theologian-philosopher and companion of Imam al-Sadiq (AS), presents a systematic epistemological argument for why God cannot be comprehended through human cognition. He categorizes all sensory perception into three types — penetration (hearing, smell, taste), contact (touch), and non-contact (vision) — and argues that even vision requires a material medium (air) and cause (light) to function. He then extends this to the heart/intellect, whose domain is confined to what exists in the material atmosphere. Directing the heart toward the Divine through imaginative contemplation inevitably results in constructing a mental image drawn from material experience, not from God Himself. This argument, delivered in an early Islamic context shaped by intense kalam (theological) debate about God's nature and attributes, was aimed at refuting both anthropomorphism and the claim that God is knowable through rational imagination alone.
